summary: At about 15:10 UTC the redis-cache hit ratio fell from about 0.96 to 0.35. The same minute, the logs show 8000 hot keys expiring within one second, and this repeats about every 20-30 seconds through 15:20. Postgres pool_waiting rose from 0 to 35 at the same time, consistent with the cache misses falling through to postgres, which portfolio-svc calls with weight 0.8. This is the most likely cause of the slowness, but the evidence is partly indirect. portfolio-svc and web-app latency summaries over 14:30-15:30 show no clear rise (max 156 ms and 178 ms), which disagrees with the reported slowness, so I prefer the measurements and flag the gap. No deploy, config, migration or flag change falls near 15:10, so what is synchronizing the TTL expiry is unknown.

hypotheses.statement: A synchronized mass expiry of about 8000 hot keys in redis-cache, repeating every 20-30 s, collapsed the hit ratio. The resulting misses hit postgres, whose connection pool saturated (pool_waiting 35), slowing portfolio and balance reads (cache stampede).
hypotheses.label: medium

supporting.text: redis-cache hit ratio was normal at 15:05 and collapsed at 15:10
hit ratio stayed at the floor afterwards
redis-cache logged a mass TTL expiry burst at onset
postgres pool_waiting rose from 0 at 15:05 to 24.5 at 15:10, then 35
portfolio-svc depends mostly on postgres and also uses redis-cache
redis memory was not under pressure, so the key loss came from TTL expiry rather than memory eviction

hypotheses.statement: postgres connection-pool saturation is an independent or amplifying bottleneck, with the pool size or slow queries unable to absorb the extra miss load.
hypotheses.label: low

unresolved: What triggered the simultaneous expiry of 8000 hot keys at about 15:10, and why it repeats every 20-30 s
Why portfolio-svc and web-app latency summaries show no clear rise even though users report slowness; the metrics may be too coarse or the impact may sit on specific endpoints
Whether postgres pool exhaustion is caused only by cache misses, because no postgres logs or query-level data were examined
The redis-cache WARN logs were truncated (52 matches, 30 shown), so burst frequency after 15:20 is unseen

actions.text: Stop the synchronized expiry. Find what sets or refreshes the TTL on the hot keys (cache-warming job, bulk write or flush) and apply jittered or longer TTLs. If a job is re-caching with identical TTLs, pause it.
actions.rationale: The expiry bursts repeat and keep the hit ratio at 0.35, so this is the likely source of the load shift to postgres.

actions.text: Relieve postgres pool pressure: raise the pool limit or add request coalescing/rate limiting on portfolio-svc cache-miss reads until the hit ratio recovers.
actions.rationale: pool_waiting is pinned at 35 and portfolio-svc sends 80% of its calls to postgres.

actions.text: Check user-facing latency with request-level or p95/p99 data for portfolio-svc and web-app, and look for per-endpoint slowness.
actions.rationale: The service-level latency summaries do not show the reported slowness, so the user impact is not yet measured directly.

actions.text: Find why the TTL expiry synchronized at 15:10. Review key-population jobs, app-level cache code, and any redis config or manual commands, since the change feed shows nothing near onset.
actions.rationale: The trigger is unidentified, and the feed has no change near 15:10.
